title: Local anaesthetics: why pain goes first and movement last
ariaLabel: Schematic of nerve conduction: local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels, so impulses stop. Thin pain fibres are blocked first, touch fibres need more, and thick motor fibres are blocked last. A light block removes pain and leaves movement; a heavy block removes all three.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or lipid value is shown or implied.

edges.label: conduction
edges.info: Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from inside the nerve, so impulses cannot be conducted. Thin pain fibres are blocked at the lowest strength.
This signal reaches the brain or muscle unless the nerve is blocked.

edges.label: conduction
edges.info: Touch and pressure fibres need a stronger block than pain fibres.
This signal reaches the brain or muscle unless the nerve is blocked.

edges.info: Large motor fibres are the last to be blocked, so a light block leaves movement.

sources: Where it acts. Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from inside the nerve; small thin fibres are blocked before large thick ones. This is standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Ionisation and pKa, vasoconstrictors, toxicity (cardiac and neurological) and lipid rescue, esters and amides, sympathetic block, antiarrhythmic use (lidocaine) and which technique suits which operation are left out. Fibre types are grouped into three. Levels and the size of each effect are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
